items.prompt: An ECS service is CPU-bound while memory remains low and task count is stable. Which task change should be tested?

options.text: Increase task CPU or choose a compatible capacity shape, then benchmark duration, cost, scheduling capacity, and service scaling.
Increase only task memory because CPU utilization is independent of task sizing.
Increase desired count without checking whether each task is under-sized.
Add EBS capacity to a Fargate task to create CPU.

feedback.Reason: Container task CPU and memory are explicit resource requests and must be sized from the measured bottleneck.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS task definitions reserve or request CPU and memory, while service count controls horizontal capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner tests per-task resource size and count against throughput, placement, cost, and downstream load.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory does not add CPU, more under-sized tasks can increase overhead, and storage does not provide compute.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Bigger tasks may improve efficiency but reduce placement granularity and increase replacement blast radius.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Memory allocation is not a substitute for a CPU bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More tasks can help but may not fix per-task saturation or dependency limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Fargate storage does not add CPU capacity.

items.prompt: An ECS container is killed for out-of-memory while host CPU is idle. What is the likely correction?
constraints: The container memory limit is observable.
The workload has a bounded working set.
The task can be resized or scaled.

options.text: Measure the container working set and increase task memory or reduce per-task load, then validate placement, cost, and scaling behavior.
Increase host CPU because OOM is always a processor issue.
Disable the memory limit so the container can consume all cluster capacity.
Add a load balancer without changing task memory or count.

feedback.Reason: Container memory limits can cause OOM independently of host CPU utilization.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS task and container memory settings constrain the process even when other host resources are idle.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect profiles heap and cache use, sets a safe limit with headroom, and scales tasks or code as needed.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU does not add memory, removing limits creates noisy-neighbor risk, and a load balancer does not fix per-task OOM.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More memory improves stability but can increase task cost and reduce placement density.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU and memory are separate resource constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded memory usage can exhaust the host and other tasks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Traffic distribution cannot fix a task that cannot hold its working set.

items.prompt: A Fargate task needs more CPU and memory than its current task size permits. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The workload fits Fargate's execution model.
The service has a latency or throughput target.

options.text: Choose a supported Fargate CPU and memory combination, then measure task startup, steady-state performance, cost, and service scaling.
Set arbitrary CPU and memory values because Fargate accepts every combination.
Use privileged host access to make the task larger.
Increase desired count without checking per-task resource fit.

feedback.Reason: Fargate task sizing uses supported CPU and memory combinations and should be validated as a service unit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Fargate abstracts servers but constrains task size and charges for requested resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects a valid shape, checks startup and placement behavior, and compares task size with horizontal scaling.
Details.errorCorrection: Unsupported combinations fail deployment, privileged host access does not change task shape, and more small tasks may increase overhead.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Larger tasks can improve efficiency while reducing fine-grained scaling and increasing failure blast radius.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Fargate has documented task size combinations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Fargate does not expose arbitrary host controls for task sizing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Desired count cannot compensate for an invalid or inefficient task shape without testing.

items.prompt: An ECS EC2 cluster has idle CPU overall but cannot place new tasks because available instances lack the requested memory shape. What should change?

options.text: Add compatible instance shapes or capacity providers, tune task sizing and placement, and monitor bin-packing, memory, CPU, and scale-out latency.
Increase cluster CPU only because total CPU is the capacity metric.
Remove task memory requests so every task can place without limits.
Add a load balancer because placement is a routing problem.

feedback.Reason: Cluster placement depends on the resource shape available on individual instances, not only aggregate CPU.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS schedules tasks against instance-level CPU, memory, ports, and other requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects compatible instance families and capacity providers and verifies task placement under growth and failure.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU-only capacity cannot satisfy memory shape, removing requests risks OOM, and a load balancer does not create hosts.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More instance diversity improves placement but increases fleet and AMI operations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Aggregate CPU does not guarantee an individual task's memory placement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Resource requests protect correctness and cannot be removed casually.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Routing does not solve insufficient scheduler capacity.

items.prompt: An ECS service scales on CPU, but request latency rises while CPU remains low because requests wait on a downstream pool. Which target should be considered?
constraints: A useful service metric can be emitted.

options.text: Scale from a metric tied to useful work or latency and protect the downstream pool, while retaining CPU and memory as supporting signals.
Scale only on CPU because it is always proportional to user latency.
Increase desired count without checking downstream connection capacity.
Disable health checks so slow tasks remain available.

feedback.Reason: Scaling should follow the resource or work signal that predicts the user SLO, not an unrelated average metric.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CPU can be low while a queue, connection pool, or dependency is saturated; service autoscaling supports custom metrics and target tracking patterns.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner emits concurrency or latency signals, caps downstream load, and tests scale-out and scale-in delay.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU is not universally proportional to latency, extra tasks can overload dependencies, and health checks expose bad capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Custom metrics add observability work but align capacity with user demand.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU can be low at a dependency or queue bottleneck.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More tasks can increase connection pressure and worsen latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks are needed to remove unhealthy capacity.

items.prompt: An ECS service scales too slowly because requests arrive in bursts before CPU rises. What should be reviewed?
constraints: The service has a p99 target.

options.text: Use a leading metric such as request count per target or queue depth, add scheduled or step scaling where appropriate, and include task startup time in the policy.
Increase the CPU target threshold so scaling starts later.
Remove minimum capacity to make scaling fully reactive.
Scale only after the load balancer reports 5xx errors.

feedback.Reason: Reactive scaling needs a leading signal and enough warm capacity to cover launch delay.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS service autoscaling policies react to CloudWatch metrics while task startup creates a response delay.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner models arrival rate, target capacity, warm-up, cooldown, and p99 behavior and tests burst scenarios.
Details.errorCorrection: Later scaling worsens latency, zero minimum capacity adds cold capacity delay, and 5xx is a late signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warm capacity costs more but protects burst latency; predictive scaling needs a reliable demand signal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A higher threshold delays response to the burst.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Scale-from-zero cannot cover immediate demand without startup time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Error-driven scaling reacts after the SLO has already failed.

items.prompt: A stateless ECS service can tolerate task replacement and wants lower EC2 cost. Which capacity provider strategy should be evaluated?
constraints: The service spans more than one capacity pool.

options.text: Evaluate a capacity provider strategy that mixes compatible On-Demand and Spot capacity with deployment, interruption, and minimum-capacity safeguards.
Use only Spot for a service that cannot tolerate task interruption.
Use only one Spot pool to avoid scheduling complexity.
Disable deployment health checks because tasks are replaceable.

feedback.Reason: ECS capacity providers can express capacity mix while the service retains interruption and deployment safeguards.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Capacity providers and strategies map tasks to EC2 or Fargate capacity with different cost and interruption behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps baseline On-Demand capacity, diversifies Spot, and tests draining, replacement, and deployment.
Details.errorCorrection: All-Spot service can lose capacity, one pool concentrates risk, and health checks remain essential.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Spot lowers cost but creates interruption and scaling variability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Interruption-tolerant does not mean interruption-free.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Diversification reduces one-pool capacity risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replaceable tasks still need healthy deployment and routing checks.

items.prompt: An ECS deployment takes too long to scale because every new task pulls a large image. What should be optimized?

options.text: Reduce image size and layer churn, place the registry path appropriately, pre-warm capacity where needed, and measure pull and application startup separately.
Increase task desired count only after the burst has started.
Put secrets directly into the image to avoid startup calls.
Use a larger database to make image pulls faster.

feedback.Reason: Container startup includes image pull and initialization, which can dominate scale-out latency.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS tasks must obtain image layers and initialize before serving traffic; image and registry locality affect time.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner uses small immutable images, caches or prewarms where supported, and sets autoscaling targets with startup delay included.
Details.errorCorrection: Reactive desired count is late, secrets in images are unsafe, and database size is unrelated.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Image optimization improves startup but requires build discipline and layer compatibility.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Adding desired count after demand arrives does not remove pull latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Secrets in images create leakage and rotation problems.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Database capacity does not affect image transfer.

items.prompt: An ECS EC2 cluster has sufficient CPU but cannot place tasks because ENI or private-IP capacity is exhausted. What should be reviewed?
constraints: Network density is the placement limit.

options.text: Evaluate instance ENI and IP limits, subnet capacity, task networking mode, instance family, and scale-out topology rather than adding CPU alone.
Increase memory because ENI capacity is proportional to RAM.
Disable awsvpc isolation to avoid all network limits without checking security.
Use a larger EBS volume to create private IP addresses.

feedback.Reason: Container placement can be limited by network interfaces and IP addresses independently of compute resources.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: awsvpc tasks consume ENI or private-IP capacity and subnets have finite address space and instance limits.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect calculates task density, reserves subnet headroom, and chooses supported instance networking capacity.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory does not add ENIs, removing isolation changes security, and EBS does not allocate network addresses.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher network density can improve packing but creates subnet and failure-domain planning needs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Network attachment limits are distinct from memory.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Networking mode is a security and connectivity contract, not a free capacity switch.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Storage does not create IP addresses.

items.prompt: An ECS rolling deployment must maintain availability while replacing old tasks. Which parameters need sizing?
constraints: The service has a minimum healthy target.

options.text: Set deployment minimum and maximum healthy percentages from capacity, startup, health-check, and rollback behavior, then test the deployment under load.
Stop all old tasks first to free capacity.
Set maximum healthy capacity to unlimited without cluster headroom.
Disable health checks so tasks count as ready immediately.

feedback.Reason: Rolling deployment capacity and health timing determine whether an update preserves service or stalls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS deployment configuration controls how many old and new tasks can coexist while health checks determine readiness.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner reserves headroom, observes startup and health time, and verifies automatic rollback and traffic behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Stopping old tasks causes an availability gap, unlimited max can exhaust capacity, and health checks protect correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Extra deployment capacity costs more but reduces rollout duration and failure risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Removing healthy capacity before replacement creates an outage risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Cluster capacity is finite and max surge must be bounded.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unhealthy tasks must not receive traffic.

items.prompt: A Fargate task downloads temporary data larger than its current ephemeral disk and fails before processing. What is the correction?
constraints: The platform supports the required storage size.
The task has a bounded working set.

options.text: Configure the task's supported ephemeral storage size and validate image, scratch, and output behavior against the task's memory and duration budget.
Increase task CPU because storage capacity follows CPU automatically.
Use the container image filesystem as unlimited writable storage.
Store temporary data in environment variables.

feedback.Reason: Fargate temporary storage is a separate task resource with a configured capacity and lifecycle.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Fargate tasks have ephemeral storage for image and runtime scratch, which is lost with the task.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sizes it from peak temporary bytes and keeps durable results in a persistent service.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU does not add disk, image layers are not unlimited writable storage, and environment variables are configuration.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Larger ephemeral storage supports workloads but does not provide durable recovery.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU and ephemeral storage are separate resources.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Image storage and writable task storage have limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Environment variables cannot hold arbitrary temporary datasets safely.

items.prompt: A container service has high CPU and disk use after verbose logging was enabled. What should be reviewed?
constraints: Local disk and CPU are finite.

options.text: Measure log volume and serialization cost, set retention and sampling, use an appropriate log driver or sidecar, and preserve required audit events.
Disable all logging to restore performance.
Increase task count without reducing per-task logging overhead.
Store unbounded logs on ephemeral task disk as the source of truth.

feedback.Reason: Logging can consume container CPU, memory, disk, network, and downstream ingestion capacity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Container logs are generated and shipped through a configured path with finite task and service resources.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner keeps required audit records, samples debug data, sets retention, and monitors log delivery and task health.
Details.errorCorrection: No logging harms diagnosis and compliance, more tasks multiply total log volume, and ephemeral disk is not durable history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Sampling lowers cost and overhead but must retain security and failure evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Removing all telemetry creates an operational and audit blind spot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More tasks can multiply the same logging overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Task disk is ephemeral and bounded.

items.prompt: An ECS service has healthy tasks but callers see intermittent connection failures after scaling. Which path should be tested?

options.text: Validate service discovery or load-balancer registration, DNS TTL, security groups, health checks, connection reuse, and task startup or drain timing.
Increase task CPU because DNS failures are always compute saturation.
Cache task IPs forever to avoid service discovery changes.
Disable deregistration delay so active connections are dropped immediately.

feedback.Reason: Container scale changes endpoints and connection state, so discovery, health, and draining form one performance path.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS tasks receive dynamic IPs or registrations and callers may cache DNS or hold connections beyond task lifecycle.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect tests registration and draining, uses appropriate TTL and retries, and avoids stale endpoint assumptions.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU does not explain discovery failure, infinite IP caching creates stale calls, and dropping connections harms availability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Shorter discovery or drain times improve turnover but can increase lookup and retry traffic.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Service discovery and registration are separate from task CPU.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Endpoint caches must respect replacement and TTL behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Graceful draining protects active requests.

items.prompt: A deployment kills tasks while requests are still in flight. Which container behavior should be implemented?

options.text: Implement graceful shutdown and signal handling, configure deregistration and stop timeouts, and test in-flight request completion before task termination.
Terminate the process immediately so deployment finishes faster.
Increase desired count without draining old tasks.
Retry every request from the client without idempotency.

feedback.Reason: Graceful task draining protects in-flight requests during replacement and scale-in.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS service deployments and load balancers expose deregistration and stop timing that must align with application signal handling.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner stops accepting new work, finishes bounded requests, and validates deployment and scale-in under load.
Details.errorCorrection: Immediate termination drops work, extra tasks do not protect connections on killed nodes, and retries can duplicate side effects.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer drain time can slow scale-in and deployment but reduces request loss.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Immediate termination creates connection and request failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Old tasks still need a graceful drain path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retries require idempotency and can multiply side effects.

items.prompt: A production ECS service must tolerate an AZ failure and should not place all tasks on one host. Which service configuration matters?
constraints: Host and AZ distribution are measurable.

options.text: Use multi-AZ subnets and placement or capacity strategies that distribute tasks across hosts and zones, then test failure and replacement behavior.
Place all tasks on one large host to minimize network hops.
Use one subnet because a service is automatically multi-AZ.
Disable task health checks after distribution is configured.

feedback.Reason: Container availability depends on host and AZ distribution plus health and replacement behavior.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS placement constraints and strategies influence task distribution, while subnets determine AZ placement.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets spread or balanced strategies, verifies spare capacity, and simulates host and AZ loss.
Details.errorCorrection: A single host is a SPOF, one subnet can be one AZ, and distribution does not replace health checks.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Spread can reduce packing efficiency and increase cost but limits correlated failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One host creates correlated task failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A subnet belongs to one AZ and does not imply multi-AZ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks remain necessary after placement.

items.prompt: An ECS service has no spare EC2 capacity for a rolling deployment. What should be corrected?
constraints: Old and new tasks must overlap.
The deployment has an availability objective.

options.text: Reserve cluster headroom or tune deployment maximum and minimum healthy percentages with capacity providers, then test rollout and rollback.
Stop healthy tasks before launching replacements.
Set the maximum healthy percentage to zero.
Disable the deployment circuit breaker.

feedback.Reason: Rolling deployments need capacity for overlap or an explicitly staged replacement strategy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS deployment percentages determine how many tasks can coexist and the cluster must place them.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner reserves capacity, sets failure detection and rollback, and validates rollout under real task startup time.
Details.errorCorrection: Stopping healthy tasks creates an availability gap, zero max prevents replacement, and disabling circuit breaking hides failed deploys.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Headroom costs more but reduces deployment risk and duration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Healthy capacity should remain until replacement is ready.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: No surge capacity can stall or serialize the deployment.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Circuit breakers help expose and stop unhealthy rollouts.

items.prompt: A container process is running but is not serving requests, and the service keeps routing traffic to it. Which control is missing?
constraints: Application health differs from process health.
The load balancer can use health checks.

options.text: Configure an application-aware container or load-balancer health check with a bounded timeout and replacement behavior, then test startup and dependency failures.
Use process existence as the only health signal.
Increase desired count without removing unhealthy tasks.
Disable health checks to improve task startup time.

feedback.Reason: A running process is not equivalent to a healthy service endpoint.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS and load balancers can use health checks to gate traffic and replace unhealthy tasks.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks the readiness dependency boundary, sets grace periods, and verifies bad tasks leave service.
Details.errorCorrection: Process-only checks miss deadlocked or dependency-failed apps, extra tasks can include bad capacity, and no checks route failures.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep checks can add dependency load and startup time, so they need careful scope and grace periods.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A process can be alive while the endpoint is unusable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Desired count does not remove unhealthy tasks unless health is observed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks are essential for correct routing and replacement.

items.prompt: A service has predictable weekday bursts and task image pulls take minutes. What capacity design should be evaluated?

options.text: Keep a measured warm capacity floor or scheduled scaling, optimize image startup, and use target scaling for residual demand.
Scale from zero for a sub-minute p99 requirement despite multi-minute startup.
Keep maximum capacity permanently without cost review.
Increase health-check interval until slow tasks appear healthy.

feedback.Reason: Predictable bursts and long startup favor pre-provisioned capacity plus reactive scaling.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Capacity provider and service scaling have warm-up and image-pull delays that affect latency SLOs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner schedules a baseline, measures startup, and sets scale-out and scale-in thresholds from demand and cost.
Details.errorCorrection: Scale-from-zero cannot meet an earlier-than-startup SLO, maximum capacity wastes money, and loose checks hide readiness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Warm capacity costs idle resources but protects burst response.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Startup delay is longer than the target response window.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A permanent maximum is not cost-aware.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health checks must reflect readiness, not hide delay.

items.prompt: An ECS task definition allocates CPU shares but the service still experiences contention on a busy EC2 host. What should be checked?
constraints: CPU limits or reservations are configured.
The service has a latency target.

options.text: Review task CPU reservation or limit semantics, host capacity, placement density, noisy neighbors, and whether a larger task or isolated capacity is needed.
Assume CPU settings guarantee dedicated physical cores on every launch type.
Remove CPU limits so one task can consume all host capacity.
Add memory to prevent all CPU contention.

feedback.Reason: ECS CPU settings have launch-type and reservation semantics and do not always mean dedicated cores.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Task CPU reservations and limits interact with host scheduling and other tasks on EC2 or Fargate.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner validates effective allocation, adjusts task shape or density, and isolates noisy workloads where necessary.
Details.errorCorrection: Dedicated-core behavior cannot be assumed, unbounded CPU causes noisy-neighbor failure, and memory does not add CPU.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Isolation improves predictability but can reduce packing efficiency and increase cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU allocation semantics depend on launch type and configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unbounded consumption harms other tasks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Memory allocation is a separate resource.

items.prompt: An ECS service scales out and the database reaches its connection quota before task CPU is high. What is the architectural correction?
constraints: Request rate and pool size are measurable.

options.text: Bound per-task pools, use connection multiplexing or a proxy where appropriate, scale from database capacity, and monitor connections and latency.
Add unlimited tasks because horizontal scaling always reduces database load.
Increase task memory and leave connection count unlimited.
Disable database connection errors so tasks remain healthy.

feedback.Reason: Container elasticity can amplify downstream connection demand and needs an explicit pool and database capacity model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Task count multiplied by per-task connections can exceed database or proxy limits independently of CPU.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner calculates connection budget, caps task pools, and scales service and database together.
Details.errorCorrection: Unlimited tasks amplify connections, memory does not raise database quota, and masking errors creates false health.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pooling or a proxy adds a component but protects the database and makes scaling predictable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More tasks can multiply database connections and worsen saturation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Memory does not change database connection quota.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Errors must remain observable and trigger controlled recovery.

items.prompt: A container service is scaled only from host CPU and misses user latency during queue growth. What metric should be added?
constraints: Queue depth or request concurrency is observable.
Host CPU is not correlated with demand.

options.text: Use a service-level metric such as request count per target, queue age, or concurrency that tracks useful work, and validate scale delay and downstream capacity.
Use host CPU only because service metrics are too application-specific.
Scale from log volume without relating it to work or latency.
Scale from the number of deployments.

feedback.Reason: Application-aware demand metrics provide a better scaling signal when host utilization is not predictive.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS Service Auto Scaling can use CloudWatch metrics and target tracking from service workload signals.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner emits a stable metric, sets cooldown and capacity bounds, and tests demand and dependency response.
Details.errorCorrection: Host CPU can be low at a queue bottleneck, logs are an indirect signal, and deployments do not measure demand.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Custom metrics require instrumentation and cardinality control but improve SLO alignment.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Host CPU is not the measured demand signal in this scenario.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Log volume can change without useful work or latency correlation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deployment count is unrelated to request load.

items.prompt: A review compares ECS on EC2, ECS on Fargate, and Kubernetes on EKS for a service with variable load. What should decide the choice?
constraints: Latency, capacity, and cost are measurable.

options.text: Compare workload resource shape, host or platform control, startup and scaling time, networking, storage, observability, team operations, availability, and unit cost.
Choose the service with the smallest control plane regardless of workload requirements.
Choose EC2 because containers always need host management.
Choose Fargate because serverless containers have unlimited resources and zero startup delay.

feedback.Reason: Container platforms trade host control, operations, resource shapes, elasticity, and cost.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ECS EC2, Fargate, and EKS have different scheduling, node, networking, storage, and operational contracts.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects one canonical platform from measured service needs and team capability, then validates scaling and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Platform choice is not only control-plane size, containers can run without customer-managed hosts, and Fargate has finite resources and startup time.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A managed data plane reduces host operations but can constrain low-level control and shape choices.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Control-plane effort is only one part of workload fit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Fargate can run containers without customer-managed hosts.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Serverless containers still have documented resource and startup limits.
